chapter: Split, hospital and decline of tap
title: Freddie James' heel work and handstand split
summary: Green compares Steele's heels to Freddie James, who did handstands onto his heels and a modern split, including a Step Brothers film scene.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Using the heels like that, Chuck, also reminds me of what we saw you do a little earlier, when you did --
Freddy James, with the heels -- lots and lots of heels.

Yes. It was -- it was introduced by him, you know. He called it enclosures, see, which was in -- that's the interiors. Because he did his heels -- he would do what they call a hand stand and he would use his heels, you know, up in the sky. As he would come down from a hand stand into what they call -- well, it was almost like a Chinese flip, but not quite. What's the other -- what they call it -- the running split?
Well, we call it modern split.
Full split, which a man usually uses a modern split, which is one leg straight out and the other leg

Yeah, that's it. That's how you would come out of a hand stand. He did it in one of the east side -- I think it was the East Side Kids movie -- the Bowery Boys, something you know. With the Step Brothers -- that's what he done it with. He was a loader, you know. They had went to some stock room, you know, they had loaded the truck, you know, and they'd be tap dancing. They was doing the Step Brothers dance and while loading these properties on to this truck. And each one of them would do some kind of a tap step to get back on to the truck -- the vehicle, see, and they asked about James -- "Where's James? James -- where's James?" And he'd just be finishing off this platform as the truck goes to pull away he pulls a bit away and James comes out from the platform and head over heels from the hand stand on to the vehicle -- the truck, into this modern split, you see. And they come up -- that's it, folks.
Chuck, I just want to say one more time, as Duke would say, when you saw Peckin' Joe in the hospital and he showed you the step, did it at all remind you of Freddy James?

Well, I must agree with that question. It's a very good question, because they were -- I'd say we were all in the same parade. The tap dancers were the tap dancers, you see, and it was just their student body, you see, and they all tried to graduate, you know, or enlarge their degrees, see.
